concepts.title: Models and simulators
concepts.explanation:
A simulator is a special kind of model. It is a copy of a system or scenario that helps people develop and practise skills safely. Think about a driving simulator. A learner can practise steering, braking and turning on a screen, long before they sit in a real car on a busy Hargeisa street. If they make a mistake in the simulator, nobody is hurt and nothing is damaged - they simply try again.

Simulators are used in many important areas of life. A surgeon practises a difficult operation on a surgery simulator before ever touching a real patient, so no lives are put at risk while they learn. A pilot trains in a flight simulator before flying a real aeroplane full of passengers. Simulators are also used in space exploration, in manufacturing, and in retail to plan how a shop should be laid out. The common thread is always the same: a simulator lets you learn, test and plan without the cost or the danger of using the real system.

One of the earliest flight simulators was the Link Trainer.
concepts.example: It was created by an American inventor called Edwin Link, who began building it in 1927; it went on sale in 1929. He made it because there was a real need for a safe way to teach new pilots how to use an aeroplane's controls before they ever left the ground.

concepts.title: Features and key features
concepts.explanation:
When you use a simulator, all the information shown on the screen and all the options you can choose are called the features. In a flight simulator, the features include the speed reading, the dials, the view from the cockpit window, the buttons to change aeroplane, and the controls to steer left and right. Some features matter more than others. A key feature is one that is especially important or useful. In a flight simulator, the display that shows the aeroplane's speed is a key feature, because without knowing the speed the pilot cannot fly safely.

Learning to spot the key features of any system is a real computing skill. When you design your own models later, you will have to decide which pieces of information are the most important to show - and which are just nice extras. A good designer puts the key features where the user will notice them first.

concepts.title: Simulators and data
concepts.explanation:
A simulator cannot do anything until you give it data. Data is the information the simulator processes to produce an output. In a flight simulator, the data you input might be the speed you set with the number keys, the direction you choose with the arrow keys, and the moment you decide to take off. A real pilot inputs the same kinds of data to a real aeroplane - they set the speed and steer in different directions - just using proper controls instead of a keyboard and mouse.

Much of this data is vital. What would happen in the simulator if you never set a speed? The aeroplane would just sit still. What if you could not turn left or right? It could only fly in a straight line. This shows why choosing the right data is such an important part of any model. There is a second kind of data too: the data a programmer needs to build the simulator in the first place, such as how high and how fast the aeroplane is allowed to fly, and what controls the user will have. So data is needed both to build a model and to run it.

concepts.title: Spreadsheet models
concepts.explanation:
Now we move to the kind of model you will build yourself: a spreadsheet model. A spreadsheet is a grid of boxes called cells, arranged in lettered columns (A, B, C, ...) and numbered rows (1, 2, 3, ...). Every cell has an address made from its column letter and row number, called a cell reference. The cell in column F, row 7 is written F7. Cell references are how you tell the spreadsheet which numbers to use.

A spreadsheet becomes a model when you add formulas. A formula is an instruction that calculates a result, and in LibreOffice Calc a formula always begins with an equals sign =. Instead of typing an answer, you type a formula that works the answer out from other cells. The magic is this: when you change one of those cells, every formula that uses it recalculates instantly. That is exactly what lets a spreadsheet answer what-if questions.

You can use a spreadsheet model to analyse a business, such as Leila's stall: how much money it takes in (its revenue), how much it spends, and how much profit is left over. If the profit is too low, you can model a change - a higher price, or selling more items - and see the result before you risk it in real life. You can also analyse things like students' test scores, using formulas to find the highest, the lowest and the average score.

Here are the four functions you will use most. A function is a ready-made formula with a name.

The part in brackets, like E3:E6, is a range - it means 'every cell from E3 to E6'. The colon : is what makes it a range. Getting that colon right is important: E3:E6 means four cells, but E3-E6 would try to subtract E6 from E3, which is not what you want at all.

Formula — What it does · Example use

=SUM(E3:E6) — Adds up all the numbers from cell E3 down to E6. · Total of a column

=AVERAGE(F3:F6) — Finds the mean (adds them up, divides by how many). · Average profit

=MAX(F3:F6) — Gives the largest number in the range. · Best-selling profit
concepts.example: =MIN(F3:F6) — Gives the smallest number in the range. · Weakest profit

concepts.title: Building Leila's model in LibreOffice Calc
concepts.explanation:
Let us build Leila's stall model step by step. Open LibreOffice Calc. You will type the headings in row 2, then one row for each product. Here is exactly what the finished model looks like. The grey top row and left column show the cell references so you can see where everything goes.

The prices are in Somali shillings, written Sh for short. You type the plain facts into columns A to D (the item name, its cost to make, its selling price and how many were sold). Columns E and F, and the totals in row 7, are not typed in - they are calculated by formulas. Here are those formulas.

The formulas behind Leila's model

Let us read the profit formula for casiir, in cell F3. It is =(C3-B3)*D3. The brackets are worked out first: C3-B3 is the price minus the cost, which is 5000-2000 = 3000 shillings of profit on one cup. Then *D3 multiplies that by the number sold, 30, giving 90000. The spreadsheet shows 90000 in cell F3. The total profit in F7 uses =SUM(F3:F6), which adds 90000 + 80000 + 62500 + 30000 to give 262500 shillings.

You do not have to type the formula into every row. Type it once in E3 and F3, then use the fill handle - the small square at the bottom-right corner of the selected cell - and drag it down to row 6. Calc copies the formula and adjusts the references automatically: E3 was =C3*D3, so E4 becomes =C4*D4, E5 becomes =C5*D5, and so on. This clever behaviour is called a relative reference, and it saves you a great deal of typing.

Row — A · B · C · D · E · F

2 — Item · Cost (Sh) · Price (Sh) · Number sold · Revenue (Sh) · Profit (Sh)

3 — Casiir · 2000 · 5000 · 30 · 150000 · 90000

4 — Shaah · 1000 · 3000 · 40 · 120000 · 80000

5 — Sambuus · 1500 · 4000 · 25 · 100000 · 62500

6 — Buskut · 1000 · 2500 · 20 · 50000 · 30000

concepts.title: What
concepts.explanation:
Now the model earns its keep. What-if analysis means asking a question that begins 'What if...?', changing a value, and watching the effect ripple through the other cells. Because the formulas recalculate the instant you press Enter, you see the answer immediately. This is far faster and safer than trying a change in real life.

Leila's first question is: What if I raise the price of casiir from 5000 to 6000 shillings? To test it, click cell C3, type 6000, and press Enter. Watch what happens. The revenue in E3 jumps from 150000 to 180000. The profit in F3 climbs from 90000 to 120000, because now each cup earns 6000-2000 = 4000 shillings and she sells 30 of them. The total profit in F7 rises from 262500 to 292500. In one keystroke, Leila can see that raising the price by 1000 shillings would add 30000 shillings to her profit - if her customers are still happy to buy.
concepts.example: That last point matters. A model is only as good as the thinking behind it. The spreadsheet assumes Leila still sells 30 cups at the higher price, but in real life a higher price might mean fewer sales. A wise data manager tests several what-if questions and uses good judgement, rather than trusting one number blindly. Try more questions yourself: What if she sells 45 cups of casiir? What if the cost of sambuus rises by 500 shillings? Change the value and read the new totals.

concepts.title: The Goal Seek tool
concepts.explanation:
What-if analysis works forwards: you change an input and see the new output. But sometimes you know the output you want and need to find the input that reaches it. For that, Calc has a brilliant tool called Goal Seek. You set the goal, and Goal Seek works backwards to find the value that achieves it. In LibreOffice Calc you open it from the Tools menu: click Tools > Goal Seek.

The Goal Seek dialog has three boxes. Formula cell is the cell that holds the result you care about (it must contain a formula). Target value is the number you want that cell to reach. Variable cell is the single cell Calc is allowed to change to hit the target (it must hold a plain number, not a formula). Let us try Leila's next question.

What if Leila wants her total profit to be exactly 300000 shillings - what price must she charge for casiir? Here the goal is the total profit in F7, and the value we will let Calc change is the casiir price in C3. Fill the dialog in like this.

Goal Seek settings for Leila's 300000 profit question

Variable cell: C3 (the casiir price, which Calc will change)

Click OK. Calc asks 'Insert the result into the variable cell?' - click Yes to keep it. The casiir price in C3 changes to 6250, and the total profit in F7 now reads exactly 300000. Goal Seek has worked backwards from the goal to the answer: casiir must be sold at 6250 shillings for the stall to make 300000 shillings of total profit. You can check it by hand: (6250-2000)*30 = 127500 profit on casiir, and 127500 + 80000 + 62500 + 30000 = 300000.

Goal Seek can change any single input. Suppose instead Leila asks: How many cups of shaah must I sell to make 100000 shillings profit on shaah alone? The shaah profit is in F4, and the number sold is in D4. Set Formula cell F4, Target value 100000, Variable cell D4, and click OK. Calc sets D4 to 50, because each shaah earns 3000-1000 = 2000 shillings of profit, and 2000*50 = 100000.
concepts.example: You have learned to model data in a spreadsheet. Now you will learn to store and manage data in a database. A database is an organised store of data that you can search, sort and update quickly and reliably. Where a spreadsheet is brilliant for calculating, a database is brilliant for keeping large amounts of data tidy, accurate and easy to find.

concepts.title: Data and its purpose
concepts.explanation:
Before you collect any data, you must ask one simple question: what is it for? The purpose of data is the reason you need it. Collecting data with a clear purpose keeps your database useful; collecting data for no reason just clutters it up and can even invade people's privacy.

Imagine Sami is a helper in the Ehel Academy library, and some new volunteers are starting. To decide what jobs to give each volunteer, Sami needs some data: their name, their age, whether they have volunteered before, which tasks they enjoy, and whether they have any disability that affects lifting or carrying. Every one of those items has a clear purpose - it helps him give safe, suitable jobs. But he does not need their favourite colour or favourite drink. That data has no purpose for this task, so it should not be collected.
concepts.example: Data can also be incomplete or missing, and that causes problems. If Sami does not know that a volunteer has a back injury, he might ask them to carry a heavy box of books and cause harm. If he does not know which tasks a volunteer enjoys, he might give them a job they dislike. So a good data manager checks two things: that every item of data collected is necessary (it has a purpose), and that the data is complete (nothing important is missing).

concepts.title: The parts of a database
concepts.explanation:
A database stores its data in one or more tables. A table looks a lot like a spreadsheet grid, but the words we use are different and precise. Look at the Ehel Academy library's book-reviews table below, then we will name every part.

A field is one column of the table - all the data about one aspect of every record. ReviewerAge is a field; so is BookTitle. A record is one row of the table - all the data about a single thing. The whole of row 3 (Maya, 13, The Clever Fox, 5) is one record: everything the database knows about that one review. So fields go down as columns, and records go across as rows.

The first field, ReviewID, is special. It is the primary key: a field where every record has a unique value, so no two records can ever be mistaken for each other. Even if two students called Leila both review the same book, their reviews still have different ReviewID numbers, so the database can always tell them apart. A good primary key is never left blank and is never repeated. In LibreOffice Base you can let the database fill it in automatically, counting 1, 2, 3, 4 for you.

The word database has been used since the 1960s, when computers first became powerful enough to store large collections of data.

Today almost everything you use runs on databases: your school register, the shop that sells you a sim card in Hargeisa, the hospital that keeps your health records, and every app on a phone.

2 — Ben · 12 · Journey to the Stars · 4

3 — Maya · 13 · The Clever Fox · 5

4 — Rohan · 14 · Sailing the Red Sea · 3

concepts.title: Accurate data and consistent formats
concepts.explanation:
When you search a database, you want to find every record that matches - no more and no fewer. That only works if the data has been entered in a consistent format. The format of a field is the agreed structure of the data in it. Look at what goes wrong when a 'date of birth' field is filled in every-which-way.

Suppose you search for everyone born on 11 January 2001. If you search for 11/01/2001 you find John Jones. But Sebastian Wong was born on the very same day - his date is just written as '11th January 01', so the search misses him. Search for 11.01.2001 and you find nobody at all, because no record is written that way. The data is not wrong, exactly, but it is inconsistent, and inconsistent data gives wrong search results.

The fix is to agree one format for every field and stick to it - for example, all dates written as DD/MM/YYYY (day / month / year). In a database you enforce this by choosing the right field type (a real Date field only accepts real dates) and by adding validation, which is our next big idea.

First name — Last name · Date of birth

John — Jones · 11/01/2001

Sue — Begum · 16.06.83

Natasha — Johansson · 12th October 2002

Sebastian — Wong · 11th January 01

concepts.title: Validation
concepts.explanation:
Validation means setting rules that check data as it is entered, and rejecting anything that breaks the rules. Validation cannot tell whether data is true - it cannot know if you really are 13 - but it can stop obvious mistakes, like a blank name, a score of 99, or a phone number with letters in it. Here are the four validation checks you need to know, and how each one is done in LibreOffice Base.

Notice the last column. This is an important difference from the textbook, which uses Microsoft Access. In Access you type a rule such as Is Not Null or >=1 And <=5 into a 'Validation Rule' box. LibreOffice Base works differently and has no such box in the table designer. Instead, a presence check is the field property Entry required = Yes; a length check is the Length property of a text field; and a range check is set on the form by giving a numeric control a Min value and a Max value. The idea is identical; only the method changes.

Validation check — What it does · How you do it in LibreOffice Base

Presence check — Stops a field being left blank (empty). The simplest rule. · Field property: Entry required = Yes

Format check — Makes sure data follows a set pattern, such as a real date. · Use the correct field type (Date [DATE]) and a format

Length check — Limits how many characters may be entered in a field. · Text field property: Length (for example 25)
concepts.example: Range check — Keeps a number within set limits, such as 1 to 5. · Form control Min value / Max value (or an SQL CHECK)

concepts.title: Creating the database and its validation in LibreOffice Base
concepts.explanation:
Now you build the library database. Open LibreOffice Base. The Database Wizard appears; choose Create a new database, click Next, keep the default embedded database, then Finish, and save the file as EhelLibrary.odb. You now have an empty database. In the left panel, click Tables, then Create Table in Design View.

Design View is where you describe each field. It shows a grid with a Field Name column, a Field Type column, and a Description column, with a Field Properties panel beneath it. Type in the five fields for the book-reviews table like this.

To make ReviewID the primary key, right-click the small grey box to the left of its row and choose Primary Key; a little key icon appears. In its Field Properties, set AutoValue to Yes so Base numbers each record automatically. For the presence checks, click each of the other fields in turn and set Entry required to Yes - now none of them can be left blank. For the length check, click ReviewerName and set its Length to 25, so a name can be at most 25 characters. Save the table (press Ctrl+S) and name it BookReviews.

The range check on ReviewScore (it must be 1 to 5) is set slightly differently, because Base does this on the data-entry form rather than in the table. When you build your form (Big Idea 14), you click the box for the review score, open its Control Properties, and set Min value to 1 and Max value to 5. Now the form refuses any score below 1 or above 5. Confident students can instead add a rule directly with Tools > SQL by typing an SQL CHECK constraint, but the form method is easier and works well.

Optional: the same range check written as SQL (Tools > SQL)

ADD CHECK ( "ReviewScore" >= 1 AND "ReviewScore" <= 5 );

Field name — Field type · Key properties to set

ReviewID — Integer [INTEGER] · Primary key; AutoValue = Yes (counts 1, 2, 3 for you)

ReviewerName — Text [VARCHAR] · Entry required = Yes; Length = 25

ReviewerAge — Small Integer [SMALLINT] · Entry required = Yes; range 5 to 100

BookTitle — Text [VARCHAR] · Entry required = Yes; Length = 60
concepts.example: ReviewScore — Small Integer [SMALLINT] · Entry required = Yes; range 1 to 5

concepts.title: Searching a database with a query
concepts.explanation:
The whole point of a database is that you can search it. A search is called a query, and a query finds every record that matches a criterion - a rule such as 'the score is greater than or equal to 4'. In LibreOffice Base, click Queries, then Create Query in Design View. Add the BookReviews table, double-click the fields you want to see so they drop into the grid, and type your rule into the Criterion row under the right field. Then press F5 (or click Run Query) to see the results.

For example, the librarian asks: which reviews gave a score of 4 or more? Under the ReviewScore field you type the criterion >= 4 and run the query. Using our six records, the answer is four reviews: Leila (5), Ben (4), Maya (5) and Nora (4). Rohan (3) and Sami (2) are correctly left out. You can do the very same thing by writing SQL, the language databases understand. Switch to SQL view and type this.

A query: reviews scoring 4 or more (returns 4 records)

SELECT "ReviewerName", "BookTitle", "ReviewScore"

Read the SQL like a sentence: SELECT these fields, FROM this table, WHERE this criterion is true. In LibreOffice Base, field and table names go inside double quotes, like "ReviewScore". You can change the criterion to ask other questions. WHERE "ReviewerAge" < 13 finds the reviewers younger than 13 - that is Ben and Sami, who are both 12. WHERE "ReviewScore" = 5 finds the top reviews, Leila and Maya. You can even sort the results: adding ORDER BY "ReviewScore" DESC lists them from the highest score to the lowest.
concepts.example: The comparison operators you use in a criterion are the same ones you met in maths: < less than, > greater than, <= less than or equal to, >= greater than or equal to, = equal to, and <> not equal to. Choosing the right operator is the difference between finding the right records and finding the wrong ones, so read your criterion carefully before you run it.

concepts.title: Data collection forms
concepts.explanation:
Typing straight into a table works, but it is not friendly for other people. A data collection form is a tidy screen that gathers data one record at a time and stores it in the database. Forms are where your range check lives, and a good form makes sure people enter data correctly and in the same format every time.

In LibreOffice Base, click Forms, then Use Wizard to Create Form. The Form Wizard guides you through simple steps: choose the BookReviews table, move the fields you want onto the form with the >> button, arrange them, and click Finish. Your form appears with a labelled box for each field. To add the range check, switch the form to design mode, click the review-score box, open its Control Properties, and set Min value to 1 and Max value to 5. Now anyone can use the form to add a review, moving to a new record with the arrow at the bottom of the window.

A wizard, by the way, is simply a help tool that guides you through creating something one step at a time - like an instruction manual built into the software. You will meet wizards all over LibreOffice.

Once a form exists, you should evaluate it - judge how good it is. Ask yourself these questions about any data collection form.

Are the instructions clear, so the user knows what to do?

Are the questions in a logical order (for example, name before age)?

Is a format set, so everyone enters data the same way (all dates DD/MM/YYYY)?

Is there enough space for the user to answer each question?
concepts.example: For any multiple-choice question, are all the answer options provided?

rules.text: Every Calc formula begins with an equals sign. A range uses a colon: SUM(F3:F6) means F3, F4, F5, F6. Type raw facts yourself; let formulas work out the totals.

Goal Seek is on the Tools menu in LibreOffice Calc. Formula cell = the goal; Target value = the number you want; Variable cell = the value Calc may change. The variable cell must be a plain number, never a formula.

A field is a column; a record is a row; the primary key is unique. Presence check = Entry required Yes; Length check = the Length property; Range check = form Min/Max value. In Base SQL, put field and table names in double quotes.

Every formula in Calc starts with an equals sign. If you type C3*D3 without the =, Calc shows the letters as text instead of calculating. A range uses a colon: SUM(F3:F6) means F3, F4, F5 and F6. Type the raw facts yourself; let formulas work out the totals. That way, when a fact changes, the totals fix themselves. Big Idea 6: What-if analysis Now the model earns its keep. What-if analysis means asking a question that begins 'What if...?', changing a value, and watching the effect ripple through the other cells. Because the formulas recalculate the instant you press Enter, you see the answer immediately. This is far faster and safer than trying a change in real life. Leila's first question is: What if I raise the price of casiir from 5000 to 6000 shillings? To test it, click cell C3, type 6000, and press Enter. Watch what happens. The revenue in E3 jumps from 150000 to 180000. The profit in F3 climbs from 90000 to 120000, because now each cup earns 6000-2000 = 4000 shillings and she sells 30 of them. The total profit in F7 rises from 262500 to 292500. In one keystroke, Leila can see that raising the price by 1000 shillings would add 30000 shillings to her profit - if her customers are still happy to buy.

In LibreOffice Calc, Goal Seek lives under the Tools menu (Tools then Goal Seek). Formula cell = the goal (must hold a formula). Target value = the number you want. Variable cell = the one value Calc may change (must hold a plain number). The Microsoft Excel version calls these Set cell, To value, and By changing cell - the same idea, different words.

Presence check in Base = the field property Entry required set to Yes. Length check in Base = the Length property of a text (VARCHAR) field. Range check in Base = a form control's Min value and Max value (or an SQL CHECK). Base has no Validation Rule box like Microsoft Access.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: In your own words, what is the difference between a model and a simulator?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A model is any representation of a real system. A simulator is a type of model that copies a system so people can practise or test safely (for example a driving simulator).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: State one key feature a flight simulator should have, and say why it is a key feature.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The speed display is a key feature, because a pilot cannot fly safely without knowing the aeroplane's speed. (Any sensible key feature with a reason is fine.)

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What does what-if analysis let you do? Give one example question.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: It lets you change a value and see the effect on other values, for example 'What if I raise the price of casiir to 6000?'

reasoningPrompts.prompt: In LibreOffice Calc, explain what the Goal Seek tool does.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Goal Seek works backwards: you give it the result you want (target value) in a formula cell, and it finds the input value (in the variable cell) that reaches it.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Name the four parts of a database: give the words for a row, a column, the whole store, and the unique field.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Record (row), field (column), database (the whole store), primary key (the unique field).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why must the data in a field be in a consistent format? Give an example of a problem it prevents.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: So searches find every matching record. If dates are written differently (11/01/2001 and '11th January 01'), a search for one format misses records stored in another.
